chapter: Will Marion Cook and the Southern Syncopated Orchestra
title: Bechet's clarinet playing and the blues
summary: Bechet played clarinet in 1919, not yet soprano, and was a blues specialist; the orchestra's program listed his 'Characteristic Blues' alongside one-steps and fox-trots.

story.theme_name: The reed and horn player's craft: clarinet, sax, tone
story.community_name: Sidney Bechet: the man, the horn, the legend

blocks.x: Okay. I'd like to stay with this just for a bit because this is very important.
So Bechet was playing really the way he was playing later on when he began to record, or was it different at that time?
No, no, he played the same way. He played clarinet.
Not the soprano, because the soprano is another story. He started the soprano. I was with him when he got his first soprano in London.
Oh, good. Oh, we'll go into that, because I want to hear about that.
But he was pretty much playing
Oh, yes, he played. He was wonderful. He played -- Bechet was a specialist of the blues.
'Cause the blues, the number -- see it on that program, because it's marked on that. "Characteristic Blues," by Sidney Bechet. It's only a typed copy. that I made myself, but I mean it's valuable.
I'll spend tomorrow morning trying to find out what I did with it. I can't understand, 'cause it should be --
So Bechet was playing a lot of blues as solos, was it, or was it more of an ensemble?
You see, the band, they played blues as well. They played blues. They played what you'd call, in those days, we called them "quick-steps," or "one-steps",
and fox-trots. Of course in the dance schools we played "schottisches". Do you know what a schottische is?
